content: The advent of point-of-care devices has enabled patients on oral anticoagulation therapy to perform self-testing at home. Patients who self-test can either adjust their medication based on a pre-determined dose-INR (international normalized ratio) schedule, a process referred to as self-management, or they can contact a clinic to receive guidance on appropriate dose adjustments, which is termed self-monitoring. Evidence increasingly supports that self-testing for oral anticoagulant therapy is as effective as, or superior to, standard monitoring methods. The primary objective of this review was to assess the impact of self-monitoring and self-management of oral anticoagulant therapy on thrombotic events, major hemorrhages, and all-cause mortality, in comparison to standard monitoring practices. To update the review, comprehensive searches were conducted in databases such as the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials (CENTRAL), MEDLINE, and Embase up to July 1, 2015. Bibliographies were reviewed, and relevant study authors and manufacturers were contacted. No language restrictions were applied during the search process. The outcomes analyzed included thromboembolic events, all-cause mortality, major and minor hemorrhages, the proportion of tests within the therapeutic range, testing frequency, and the feasibility of self-monitoring and self-management. Data extraction was performed independently by the review authors, and statistical analyses were conducted using a fixed-effect model with the Mantel-Haenszel method. Peto’s method was used to confirm results for rare outcomes. Heterogeneity among studies was assessed using Chi-squared and I-squared statistics, and the GRADE methodology was employed to evaluate the quality of evidence. The review incorporated 28 randomized trials involving 8,950 participants, including 10 new trials with 4,227 participants added in this update. The overall quality of evidence ranged from low to moderate. Pooled data demonstrated a significant reduction in thromboembolic events with self-monitoring or self-management (RR 0.58, 95% CI 0.45 to 0.75; moderate quality evidence). Specifically, self-management trials showed a greater reduction in thromboembolic events (RR 0.47, 95% CI 0.31 to 0.70) compared to self-monitoring trials (RR 0.69, 95% CI 0.49 to 0.97), with both interventions supported by moderate-quality evidence. No significant reduction in all-cause mortality was observed overall (RR 0.85, 95% CI 0.71 to 1.01; moderate quality evidence). However, self-management trials demonstrated a significant reduction in all-cause mortality (RR 0.55, 95% CI 0.36 to 0.84), whereas self-monitoring trials did not (RR 0.94, 95% CI 0.78 to 1.15). The quality of evidence for both interventions was moderate. In 20 trials involving 8,018 participants, neither self-monitoring nor self-management significantly reduced the risk of major hemorrhage (RR 0.95, 95% CI 0.80 to 1.12; moderate quality evidence). Similarly, no significant difference was observed for minor hemorrhages (RR 0.97, 95% CI 0.67 to 1.41; low quality evidence), with the evidence downgraded due to a high risk of bias and substantial heterogeneity (I² = 82%). In conclusion, self-monitoring and self-management of oral anticoagulation therapy can enhance the quality of anticoagulation control. Both approaches were associated with a reduction in thromboembolic events. Self-management, in particular, was linked to a reduction in all-cause mortality, whereas self-monitoring was not. Neither intervention had a significant impact on the incidence of major hemorrhages.
